questions.title: Diarrhea is not an atropine adverse effect
questions.question: Adverse effects which frequently occur during treatment with high doses of atropine include all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Atropine, a muscarinic antagonist, reduces rather than increases gastrointestinal motility. This is why it is combined with diphenoxylate as an antidiarrheal, not why it causes diarrhea, making diarrhea the one effect that does NOT belong on this adverse-effect list.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Urinary retention, from reduced detrusor muscle tone, is a genuine and frequent atropine adverse effect, part of its systemic antimuscarinic profile.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dry mouth, from reduced salivary secretion, is one of the most characteristic atropine adverse effects and a genuine member of this list.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sandy or dry eyes, from reduced lacrimation and impaired accommodation, are also a real atropine adverse effect, consistent with its systemic antimuscarinic action.

questions.learning_objective: State that diarrhea is not an atropine adverse effect, since atropine reduces rather than increases GI motility.

questions.title: Blurred vision is an atropine adverse effect
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverse effect of atropine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine reduces, not increases, salivation -- dry mouth, the opposite effect, is the genuine atropine adverse effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atropine's mydriasis tends to raise, not decrease, intraocular pressure, and can precipitate an attack in narrow-angle glaucoma rather than lowering pressure.
explanations.C: Correct. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors controlling accommodation, impairing the ciliary muscle's ability to focus for near vision. Combined with its mydriasis and reduced lacrimation, this produces blurred vision as a genuine and characteristic atropine adverse effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atropine blocks the vagal (muscarinic) restraint on the heart, producing tachycardia at clinically relevant doses, not bradycardia.

questions.learning_objective: State that blurred vision, from impaired accommodation, is an atropine adverse effect.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Blurred vision"

questions.title: Physostigmine reverses the anticholinergic toxidrome
questions.question: A patient presents at Assiut University Hospital with high fever, hallucinations, marked mydriasis, and a dry mouth after ingesting an unknown drug. To counteract the effects of the drug you prescribe:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A cholinesterase reactivator (like pralidoxime) treats organophosphate poisoning by reactivating an inhibited enzyme, not the antimuscarinic toxidrome described here, which involves no enzyme inhibition to reverse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. NSAIDs treat pain and inflammation, not an anticholinergic toxidrome's fever, hallucinations, mydriasis and dry mouth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A parasympatholytic (an antimuscarinic) would worsen, not counteract, this presentation, since the patient's symptoms are already caused by excess antimuscarinic action.
explanations.D: Correct. Fever, hallucinations, marked mydriasis and dry mouth together describe the anticholinergic toxidrome. A centrally-acting cholinomimetic -- physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier -- raises acetylcholine both centrally and peripherally, directly reversing the antimuscarinic block causing this picture.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the anticholinergic toxidrome and state that a centrally-acting cholinomimetic (physostigmine) is its treatment.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: a centrally-acting cholinomimetic"

questions.title: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist
questions.question: What type of drugs is scopolamine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Scopolamine blocks, rather than stimulates, muscarinic receptors -- a muscarinic agonist would produce miosis and increased secretion, the opposite of scopolamine's effects.
explanations.B: Correct. Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist (antimuscarinic) that, unlike atropine's more peripherally weighted action, penetrates the CNS well. This CNS penetration is what lets it prevent motion sickness and produce central effects like sedation and, in overdose, the anticholinergic toxidrome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nicotinic antagonists (such as ganglion blockers like trimethaphan) act at a different receptor and site -- the autonomic ganglion -- not the postsynaptic muscarinic receptors scopolamine blocks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nicotinic agonists stimulate, rather than block, nicotinic receptors at the ganglion or neuromuscular junction, an entirely different receptor and action from scopolamine's.

questions.learning_objective: Classify scopolamine as a CNS-penetrant muscarinic antagonist.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Muscarinic antagonists"

questions.title: Ipratropium is the next COPD option after beta2-agonist failure
questions.question: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was prescribed a β2 agonist for the relief of bronchospasm. However, the patient did not respond to this treatment. Which of the following drugs or classes of drugs would you suggest for this patient as the next option?

explanations.A: Correct. Ipratropium, an inhaled antimuscarinic bronchodilator, blocks muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle rather than repeating the beta2-adrenergic mechanism. This makes it a rational, mechanistically distinct next option for a COPD patient who does not respond to a beta2 agonist alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A muscarinic agonist would stimulate bronchoconstriction, worsening rather than relieving this patient's bronchospasm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beta1 receptors are concentrated in the heart, not the airway, so a beta1 agonist has minimal bronchodilator effect and would not help.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Physostigmine is a centrally-acting cholinesterase inhibitor used for anticholinergic toxidrome reversal, with no established bronchodilator role in COPD.

questions.learning_objective: State that ipratropium is the next bronchodilator option for a COPD patient unresponsive to a beta2 agonist.

questions.title: Muscarinic antagonists decrease urination
questions.question: Urination in the human subject is decreased by

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spider venom (such as latrodectus toxin) typically causes massive acetylcholine release, producing a muscarinic-excess picture with increased, not decreased, urination.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nicotinic agonists act at the ganglion and neuromuscular junction, not primarily at the detrusor muscarinic receptors that control bladder emptying.
explanations.C: Correct. Muscarinic antagonists reduce detrusor muscle tone by blocking the muscarinic receptors that normally mediate bladder contraction. This produces urinary retention and decreased urination. It is part of the same systemic antimuscarinic adverse-effect profile as atropine's dry mouth and reduced GI motility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. AChE inhibitors increase, rather than decrease, acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, which would increase detrusor tone and urination, not decrease it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Muscarinic agonists directly stimulate detrusor contraction, increasing rather than decreasing urination -- the opposite effect of a muscarinic antagonist.

questions.learning_objective: State that muscarinic antagonists decrease urination by reducing detrusor tone.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: muscarinic antagonists"

questions.title: Scopolamine causes mydriasis with cycloplegia, impairing near vision
questions.question: A patient presents to the physician with a dilated right eye and complains that she could not read the lunch menu with the same eye. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for her symptoms?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist, which would cause miosis (pupil constriction), not the mydriasis described in this vignette.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Timolol is a beta-blocker used for glaucoma that lowers intraocular pressure without producing mydriasis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, increases muscarinic tone and would cause miosis, the opposite of this patient's dilated pupil.
explanations.D: Correct. Scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist, produces mydriasis together with cycloplegia -- paralysis of the ciliary muscle that impairs the eye's ability to accommodate for near vision. This combination explains both the dilated pupil and her inability to read the menu with that eye.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist used to treat glaucoma by causing miosis, the opposite pupillary effect from what is described.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise scopolamine's mydriasis-with-cycloplegia effect from a clinical vignette describing impaired near vision.

questions.title: Atropine's antidiarrheal effect works by reducing GI motility
questions.question: Atropine is one of the ingredients in the antidiarrheal combination diphenoxylate/atropine available in the United States. Which of the following effects is produced by atropine that contributes to its antidiarrheal effect?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine reduces, rather than increases, secretions generally through muscarinic blockade, and acid secretion is not the mechanism behind its antidiarrheal role here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atropine reduces salivation (dry mouth is a classic adverse effect), the opposite of increased salivation, and salivary change is unrelated to its antidiarrheal action.
explanations.C: Correct. Atropine's muscarinic blockade reduces gastrointestinal motility. This slowing of gut transit is exactly what contributes to its antidiarrheal effect in the diphenoxylate/atropine combination, and is the same mechanism behind atropine's constipating adverse effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased GI motility would worsen, not treat, diarrhea -- atropine's actual effect on motility is a reduction, not an increase.

questions.learning_objective: State that atropine's reduction of gastrointestinal motility is the mechanism behind its antidiarrheal contribution.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Reduction in gastrointestinal motility."

questions.title: Trimethaphan is a ganglion blocker
questions.question: Which of the following drugs is ganglion blocker?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parathion is an organophosphate that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, producing muscarinic and nicotinic excess -- it is not a ganglion blocker.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Echothiophate is an irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor used topically for glaucoma, a different mechanism from ganglionic nicotinic-receptor blockade.
explanations.C: Correct. Trimethaphan is a ganglion blocker. It acts on nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia, blocking transmission through both the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions at that single site. This ganglionic, nicotinic-receptor mechanism distinguishes it from every muscarinic-acting drug in this lecture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist acting at postsynaptic muscarinic receptors on effector organs, not a nicotinic-receptor ganglion blocker.

questions.learning_objective: Identify trimethaphan as a ganglion blocker acting on nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia.

questions.title: Scopolamine is the most effective anti-motion sickness drug
questions.question: Which of the following drugs would be the most effective anti-motion sickness drug for a person planning to go on a cruise?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tropicamide is a short-acting antimuscarinic used topically for pupil dilation during eye examinations, not a systemic drug used for motion-sickness prevention.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Darifenacin is a bladder-selective antimuscarinic used for overactive bladder, with no established role in motion-sickness prevention.
explanations.C: Correct. Scopolamine, a CNS-penetrant muscarinic antagonist, is used specifically for prevention of motion sickness. It is classically delivered as a transdermal patch, giving sustained drug levels for exactly the kind of prolonged exposure a cruise involves. Among the antimuscarinics listed here, it is the one with this established indication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tiotropium is a long-acting inhaled antimuscarinic bronchodilator used for COPD, not a motion-sickness treatment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify scopolamine as the antimuscarinic used for motion-sickness prevention, distinct from other antimuscarinics with different clinical uses.

questions.title: Muscarinic antagonists are contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Muscarinic antagonists are useful for all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Muscarinic antagonists are contraindicated, not useful, for narrow-angle glaucoma. The pupillary dilation (mydriasis) they cause can obstruct aqueous humour outflow and precipitate an acute angle-closure attack. This worsens, rather than treats, the condition -- exactly the opposite of the other three genuine uses on this list.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscarinic antagonists are genuinely useful as an antidote for cholinergic-agonist (including organophosphate) poisoning, blocking the excess muscarinic stimulation directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Muscarinic antagonists are genuinely useful for eye examinations, since the mydriasis they cause allows a wider view of the retina.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscarinic antagonists (scopolamine specifically) are genuinely useful for preventing motion sickness, a real therapeutic use.

questions.learning_objective: State that muscarinic antagonists are contraindicated (not useful) in narrow-angle glaucoma, unlike their genuine uses as a cholinergic antidote, for eye exams and for motion-sickness prevention.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Treatment of narrow angle glaucoma"

questions.title: Anticholinergic plant poisoning resembles scopolamine toxicity
questions.question: An 11 year old boy was brought to the ER by some of his friends because he "started going crazy" after eating seeds from a plant while "trying to get high." The boy was incoherent his skin was hot and dry. His pupils were dilated and unresponsive to light. Blood pressure was 180/105 mm Hg, pulse was 150/min, and rectal temp was 40 C (104 F). The presumptive diagnosis was drug toxicity due to the ingestion of a compound similar to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cannabis intoxication does not typically produce hot, dry skin, fixed dilated pupils and severe hyperthermia together -- this specific combination points to antimuscarinic, not cannabinoid, toxicity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mescaline is a hallucinogen but does not classically produce this hot-dry-skin, fixed-mydriasis anticholinergic toxidrome.
explanations.C: Correct. Hot, dry skin, fixed dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and incoherence together describe the anticholinergic toxidrome, classically produced by plants (such as Datura/jimsonweed) containing scopolamine-like antimuscarinic alkaloids. Eating unidentified seeds "to get high" is a recognised route of exposure to exactly this class of compound.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Digoxin toxicity produces GI symptoms, visual disturbances and arrhythmias, not the hot-dry-skin, fixed-mydriasis anticholinergic picture described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication produces agitation and dissociation but not this specific combination of hot dry skin and fixed dilated pupils that marks antimuscarinic toxicity.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise plant-derived scopolamine-like antimuscarinic poisoning from its anticholinergic toxidrome presentation.
